# Hyperpigmentation disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Hyperpigmentation disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/QF0u33)

---

## Summary

<u>Hyperpigmentation</u> is an increase in <u>melanin</u> in the <u>epidermis</u> and/or <u>dermis</u>. <u>Hyperpigmentation</u> disorders are benign conditions that manifest with lesions that are darker than the adjacent <u>skin</u>. Causes of <u>hyperpigmentation</u> disorders include genetic or medical conditions and exposure to UV radiation. A detailed <u>patient history</u> and <u>skin examination</u> are required to establish the lesion type. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, further workup may include <u>skin biopsy</u> and dermatologist evaluation (e.g., with <u>Wood lamp</u>). The general <u>management of hyperpigmentation disorders</u> involves using <u>photoprotective measures</u> and addressing underlying conditions if necessary. If requested by the patient, cosmetic treatment with <u>skin lightening therapy</u> may be performed.

---

## Ephelides (freckles)

* Description: a benign type of <u>hyperpigmentation</u> with onset typically during childhood [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Etiology: genetic; precipitated by UV exposure [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[2]](/library/EmW8hN0)

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* <u>Prevalence</u> is higher among children ≥ 2 years of age and subsequently decreases with age. [[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Predominantly affects individuals with light <u>skin</u>

* Clinical features  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Well-defined <u>macules</u> of varied color (red, brown, or tan)

* 1–2 mm in size

* Number can vary from a few to hundreds

* Typically located in sun-exposed areas

* Differential diagnosis [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* <u>Juvenile lentigo</u>

* <u>Solar lentigo</u>

* Management: See “<u>Management of hyperpigmentation disorders</u>.” [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[4]](/library/FIWge50)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Ephelides</u> fade with reduced sun exposure in the winter months. [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[2]](/library/EmW8hN0)

## Solar lentigo

* Description: an acquired type of <u>hyperpigmentation</u> that affects adults  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Etiology: exposure to UV radiation [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u> is highest in adults > 40 years. [[5]](/library/G0dBho0)

* Predominantly affects individuals with light <u>skin</u> and Asian individuals [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Pathophysiology: increase in the production of <u>melanin</u>, which is then deposited in <u>basal keratinocytes</u>

* Clinical features  ;  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Yellow or brown <u>macules</u> or patches

* Typically located on sun-exposed areas (e.g., face, back of the hands)

* Number increases with age. [[2]](/library/EmW8hN0)

* Differential diagnosis [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[6]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* <u>Ephelides</u>

* <u>Seborrheic keratosis</u>

* <u>Actinic keratosis</u>

* <u>Lentigo maligna</u>

* <u>Melanoma</u>

* Management: See “<u>Management of hyperpigmentation disorders</u>.” [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

## Café au lait macules

* Description: : a benign type of <u>hyperpigmentation</u> with onset commonly at <u>birth</u> or in childhood [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Etiology: <u>idiopathic</u> or genetic (e.g., <u>neurofibromatosis</u>, <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>) [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: isolated finding in 10–30% of the general population [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Clinical features [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Well-defined tan or brown <u>macule</u> or patch

* 1–20 cm in size  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> lesions are typically solitary.

* ≥ 6 lesions suggest a genetic syndrome.  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Differential diagnosis [[7]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* <u>Becker nevus</u>

* <u>Urticaria pigmentosa</u>

* Management [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)[[4]](/library/FIWge50)

* See “<u>Management of hyperpigmentation disorders</u>.”

* If there is concern for a genetic syndrome such as <u>neurofibromatosis</u> or <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>, , refer to a specialist.

## Melasma

* Description: an acquired type of <u>hyperpigmentation</u> occurring on sun-exposed areas [[3]](/library/tIWXe50)[[8]](/library/IIWYV50)

* Etiology [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Exposure to UV radiation

* Hormonal factors, e.g.:

* <u>Pregnancy</u>: referred to as “<u>mask of pregnancy</u>” [[9]](/library/s0dtho0)

* <u>Oral contraceptive</u> use

* Medications (e.g., <u>anticonvulsant drugs</u>)

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* Common in individuals with dark <u>skin</u>

* <u>Incidence</u>: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Clinical features  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[3]](/library/tIWXe50)

* <u>Macules</u> or patches of varied color (e.g., brown or grey)

* Usually on the face (centrofacial, malar, or mandibular pattern) or forearms and bilateral

* Differential diagnoses [[7]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Actinic <u>lichen planus</u>

* <u>HIV-associated dermatological complications</u>

* <u>Contact dermatitis</u> (caused by, e.g., cosmetics)

* Management [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[4]](/library/FIWge50)[[8]](/library/IIWYV50)

* See “<u>Management of hyperpigmentation disorders</u>.”

* <u>Wood lamp</u> can show <u>skin</u> <u>enhancement</u> for lesions with an <u>epidermal</u> component.

* Treatment resistance is common; refer to a dermatologist for further management.  [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Melasma</u> usually recurs after treatment is discontinued, but it may be <u>self-limiting</u> in pregnant individuals, resolving in the <u>postpartum period</u>. [[1]](/library/XPW9Wl0)[[9]](/library/s0dtho0)
